title: The Crane That Lifts Stones
synopsis: Jeong Yak-yong's lifting machine will not lift a stone.
A note with a small water drop is tied to its rope.
goal: Find out if the lifting machine is broken, and who wrote the warning.

notes: Gwak's log, written with until / after: the wall's start (1794, fact h1) is fixed first and this morning's failure last; the machine worked until the carpenter came, and the note came after his work. The rice card is not part of it.
One order only: lift before copy (until), copy before note (after).

clueInputs.note: The same water drop as Seok's note of 1592.

learning.objective: 곽 십장의 작업 일지에서 until, after를 읽고 일이 일어난 순서를 놓아, 기계가 고장 난 것이 아니라 바뀐 것임을 알아낸다.

play.title: Broken, or Changed?
story: A big stone lies under the machine. Its ropes hang loose.
A note with a small water drop is tied to the rope.
Jeong reads its King's letters out: "The drawing is different."
play.letter:
The King's builders began the wall in 1794.
The machine lifted big stones every day, until the new carpenter came.
The new carpenter rebuilt the top from a copied drawing.
The note was on the rope after the carpenter's work.
This morning, the machine could not lift a stone.
play.question: Put the log in order. Was the machine broken, or changed?
hints: Look for the words 'until' and 'after' in the log.
What happened before the new carpenter came? What came after his work?
play.successMessage: The machine worked until someone changed it!
transition: The machine is not broken. It was changed.
"A copied drawing?" says Jeong. "Then which drawing is mine?"
He takes you to the drawing room.
play.orderFeedback: Read the log again: what came after the carpenter's work?

clue.title: Changed, Not Broken
clue.note: The machine worked until a new carpenter rebuilt its top from a copied drawing.

evidence.name: The Water-Drop Note (1795)
evidence.description: A short note in the King's letters, with a small water drop. It says: the drawing is different.

recall.title: The Same Mark?
recall.prompt: A water drop is drawn on this note. Which note in your notebook has the same mark?
recall.miss: That has no water drop. Look for a note from 1592.

play.title: Which Drawing Is Mine?
story: Three drawings of lifting machines lie on the table.
"One is mine," Jeong says. "The carpenter took the wrong one."
"Read my words, and find my drawing."
play.letter:
"My machine stands like a gate, with a beam across the top."
"Pulleys hang from the beam. More pulleys hang under them, over the stone."
"Ropes run between the pulleys, up and down."
"A big wheel stands on each side. Workers turn the wheels."
play.question: Which drawing is Jeong's?
hints: Read Jeong's first line. What shape does his machine have?
Look for pulleys in two places, and a wheel on each side.
transition: The machine in the yard has pulleys only at the top, and no wheels.
"The carpenter copied the wrong drawing," says Jeong.
"Let us rebuild it, and lift that stone."

clue.title: Jeong's Drawing
clue.value: PULLEYS ABOVE AND BELOW, A WHEEL ON EACH SIDE
clue.note: Jeong's machine is like a gate. It has pulleys in two places and two wheels.

evidence.name: Jeong's Drawing
evidence.description: A frame like a gate. Pulleys under the beam and over the stone. A wheel on each side.

options.label: Tie the ropes around the stone
Push the stone up a slope
Hook the stone to the lower pulleys

notes: Jeong's steps (made up) are written out of order with before / after / last: tie before hook, turn after hook, rise last. Two decoys (pull by hand, push up a slope) are what nobody does.

clueInputs.note: The machine is rebuilt from Jeong's drawing.

learning.objective: 정약용의 순서 설명(before, only after, last)을 읽고 돌을 들어 올리는 네 단계를 차례대로 고른다.
expressions: Before you hook the stone, tie the ropes around it.
only after the stone is hooked

play.title: The Stone Rises
story: The builders rebuild the machine from Jeong's drawing.
Now the big stone must go up onto the wall.
"Read my steps," says Jeong. "Then do them in order."
play.letter:
"Turn the two wheels only after the stone is hooked."
"Before you hook the stone, tie the ropes around it."
"The stone rises last."
"Nobody pulls the rope by hand, and nobody pushes the stone."
play.question: Tap the four steps in order.
hints: Find the step that comes before the hook.
The wheels turn only after the hook. What happens last?
play.successMessage: The wheels turn, and the stone rises!
transition: The ropes go tight. Slowly, the big stone rises onto the wall.
Gwak takes off his hat. "It was never broken," he says.
Below, a girl with a water bucket watches and smiles.

feedback.hook,tie,turn,rise: Read again: what do you do before you hook the stone?
feedback.tie,turn,hook,rise: The wheels turn only after the stone is hooked.

play.orderFeedback: Those are the right steps. Read Jeong's 'before' and 'after' again.

clue.title: The Stone Rises
clue.note: Rebuilt from Jeong's drawing, the machine lifts the stone onto the wall.

evidence.name: Jeong's Lifting Steps
evidence.description: Tie the ropes, hook the stone, turn the two wheels, and the stone rises.

notes: The answer is the real year Hwaseong was finished (s5_ep03_h1: begun in the first month of 1794, finished in the ninth month of 1796): the clerk's words give the start (also M1's fixed card) and two years and eight months. The record chest and the clerk are made up; the record book of the fortress's building (h4) and the paid workers (h5) are real.

clueInputs.note: Gwak's log: the wall began in 1794.
The machine lifts stones again: the work goes on.

learning.objective: 서기의 말(We began in the first month of 1794 … two years and eight months later)을 읽고 성이 완성된 해를 계산해 다이얼을 맞춘다.
expressions: two years and eight months later

play.title: The Record Chest
story: Autumn, 1796. Jeong invites you back to Suwon.
The last stone is on the wall.
A clerk locks a thick record book in a chest. Its lock has four number dials.
play.letter:
"This book holds every worker's name, and his pay."
"We began the wall in the first month of 1794."
"Today the work is done, two years and eight months later."
"The chest opens on the year we finished."
play.question: Turn the dials to the year Hwaseong Fortress was finished.
hints: Find the year the work began.
Count on two years from the first month. Then eight more months: is it still that year?
transition: Inside the book are thousands of names, each with its pay.
"Even the water girl is in it," laughs the clerk.

feedback.1794: That is the year the work began. Count on two years and eight months.
feedback.1795: That was the year of the stopped machine. Count on from the first month of 1794.
feedback.1797: Count again: two years and eight months after the first month of 1794.

play.orderFeedback: Those digits fit, but not in that order. Count on from 1794.

evidence.name: The Finished Fortress
evidence.description: Hwaseong was finished in 1796. Machines like the geojunggi helped lift big stones. A record book lists the workers and their pay.

ending.text: In the ninth month of 1796, Hwaseong Fortress was finished.
Machines like mine helped lift the big stones.
ending.speaker: jeong_yakyong

ending.text: A record book tells how the fortress was built.
It lists the workers, and the pay they were given.
I carry water here. I wrote the note.
ending.speaker: okbun

ending.text: Your water drop is just like Seok's, in 1592.
Seok? My mother told me that name.
ending.speaker: okbun

hook: A stone waits under a machine that will not lift.

learningGoal.title: Reading order words and how a machine is made

objectives: Put the work log in order.
Lift the stone in the right order.
intro: Spring, 1795. You are a guest of Jeong Yak-yong at Hwaseong Fortress in Suwon.
A long stone wall is rising around the new town.
Jeong designed a lifting machine, the geojunggi. It lifts heavy stones with ropes and pulleys.
But this morning, Foreman Gwak shouts across the stone yard.
"Your machine is broken! It cannot lift one stone!"
play.caseSummary: The lifting machine was not broken. A new carpenter had rebuilt it from a copied drawing. Okbun, who carries water to the builders, saw it and wrote the note. Rebuilt from Jeong Yak-yong's drawing, it lifted the stone. Hwaseong Fortress was finished in 1796. Machines like Jeong's geojunggi helped lift big stones. A record book lists the workers and their pay.

notes: PART 10 (2026-11-06), Case 03. Jeong Yak-yong is real; his words here are made up. Foreman Gwak, the new carpenter, the clerk and Okbun are made up; so are the stopped machine, the copied drawing, the three drawings and the record chest.

Ends on a checked fact: the final's answer 1796 is the year Hwaseong was finished (h1); the ending tells that machines like the geojunggi helped move and lay big stones (h2, h3) and that the record book lists the workers and their pay (h4, h5). It never says the machine made the work faster or how many pulleys it had (not checked).
